paragraphs: Five passengers boarded with invitations to the Professor’s demonstration. Who are you tonight?
What name is on your ticket?
Ada Thorne, of Thorne & Gage. You fund inventions, and you are rarely wrong. The Professor invited you to buy a stake tonight.
For your eyes only: last month the Professor begged your bank for a loan to pay his debts. You refused. If tonight’s sale had failed, you meant to buy the patent cheaply yourself.
Captain Hal Rook. You came because Colonel Marsh insisted, and because the bar on the night express is excellent.
For your eyes only: in the dark you saw Miss Vell slip out of the lounge just before the lights died. A gentleman doesn’t accuse a lady without proof.
Wren Hollis, who made a fortune in timepieces and never asks anyone where theirs came from.
For your eyes only: at dinner you lifted a brass key from the Professor’s pocket. It opens his compartment in the sleeper.
Dr. Imogen Sallow, the Professor’s physician. You came as an investor and, he joked, in case anything went wrong.
For your eyes only: last week he asked you whether a strong current could stop a weak heart. You told him yes.
. Nobody quite remembers inviting you. That is useful.

And the bruise at his temple is wrong: it came after his heart had already stopped.
“I was at the bar, as everyone saw.” He turns his glass a quarter turn.
“Dreadful business. I was at this bar the whole time.”
You mention the money. He sets the glass down. “Very well. I’m no buyer. I’m a bailiff, and that model is collateral.”
The key turns without a sound.

On the desk lies his notebook. The last entry: “Sign with Crane’s man tonight. E. must not know.” Beside a sketch of the master chronometer: “Never wind past the red mark. The coil will discharge.”
“Ardent? Brilliant fellow. Couldn’t mend a pocket watch to save his life, mind. Had a girl in the workshop for that.”
“Can’t a man sleep on this train?”
“At Coldwater someone stepped off into the rain and back on. Light step. A woman’s.”
“Let a man sleep, Rook. Ask me after Merrow.”
He grumbles awake. “At Coldwater, Rook. Someone stepped off into the rain and back on.”
Her shoes are soaked to the laces, though she swears she never left her berth.
Her eyelids flicker. She isn’t asleep.

You lay it out for everyone here: her ticket under the body, her shoes wet from Coldwater. By the next stop, the whole train has heard.
Midnight. In the observation lounge, Professor Silas Ardent lifts a brass chronometer toward the lamps. “Ladies, gentlemen: time, made portable.” He winds it once, twice—
The lights die.

Fog presses at the windows of the sleeper. Curtained berths line the corridor. At the far end, a brass plate on a locked door: S. ARDENT. Colonel Marsh sits up in a quilted gown, reading by lamplight.
The dining car smells of spilled claret. A rolled blueprint lies half under Hobbs’s tray. Mrs. Ardent sits very straight, a sealed letter by her plate.
Miss Vell passes through without a word.
Something glints beside the sugar bowl.
Your echo stands at the bar, exactly where you remember standing. You keep out of its sight.

Hobbs has laid a tablecloth over the Professor. Mr. Crane hasn’t left the bar. He watches the fog slide past the observation glass and orders another brandy.
Trunks are strapped to the walls. Behind a brass cage the generator thrums, and your watch hums faintly as you come near. At the rear, the vestibule door rattles in its frame.
Mail sacks crowd the aisle; there’s no room to run. By the sorting table sits a crate stencilled FRAGILE — PATENT OFFICE, nailed shut.
Rain drums on the roof at Coldwater. Somewhere a door to the platform opens, and closes again.
Colonel Marsh’s curtain is drawn; he snores.
Colonel Marsh is up in his gown, grumbling about the noise.
Miss Vell stands at the Professor’s door, trying the handle. She stops when she sees you.
Rain streaks the windows. Hobbs resets the tables as if nothing has happened. Mrs. Ardent has not touched her soup.
Something still glints beside the sugar bowl.
At Coldwater two railway policemen look in, see the cloth over the Professor, and are told it can wait for Kingsgate. Mr. Crane signs something for them with a flourish.
Rain hammers the roof. Through the vestibule glass: the Coldwater platform, empty but for a rain barrel under a lamp.
A woman in a dark coat bends over the rain barrel at the far end, then hurries back toward the front of the train.
New sacks swing aboard at Coldwater. On the sorting table lies a telegram: PROF. S. ARDENT, NIGHT EXPRESS. Unopened.
The rain has passed. Moonlight slides along the corridor at Merrow, and the curtains sway.
Colonel Marsh snores behind his curtain.
Miss Vell is curled in a berth, breathing slow and even.
Ash in the washbasin, and a blackened brass clasp. Someone has burned a book.
Merrow’s single lamp slides past the windows. Hobbs has set out a cold supper no one eats. Mrs. Ardent is writing a second letter.
The staff have carried the Professor to the baggage car. The demonstration table is bare, and Mr. Crane has moved one stool closer to it.
Where he lay, a ticket stub catches the lamplight.
The generator thrums. The Professor lies under a tarpaulin by the vestibule door, which rattles at every curve.
Moonlight through the slats. The crate’s label flaps loose: it comes off at Harrow Junction, the next stop.
A freight train hisses alongside at Harrow Junction, close enough to touch. The corridor shudders. Every curtain is drawn.
Behind one curtain, Miss Vell breathes slow and even.
Ash in the washbasin, and a blackened brass clasp.
The freight’s lamps strobe through the dining car. Hobbs steadies the glasses. Mrs. Ardent seals her second letter and asks him for a stamp.
Signal lamps change from red to green. Mr. Crane checks his watch, an ordinary one, against the station clock, and frowns.
A ticket stub still lies by the demonstration table.
Porters on the Harrow platform shout about the mail. Through the vestibule glass: a freight wagon, and dark fields beyond.
Miss Vell is at the vestibule door, one hand on the latch.
Two porters climb aboard for the crate marked PATENT OFFICE. At the end of this stop, it leaves the train.
Grey light at Fenwick. Colonel Marsh is up, shaving at the basin, braces dangling.
Ash in the washbasin, and a blackened brass clasp.
Hobbs lays breakfast for passengers who will not eat it. Mrs. Ardent asks whether anyone has seen Miss Vell.
Miss Vell passes through toward the mail car, gloves on.
The Fenwick platform clock reads ten to five. Mr. Crane has stopped drinking. “Whoever it was,” he says, “they had better be quick.”
The generator winds down for the terminus. Someone has left the vestibule door unlatched.
Miss Vell is at the vestibule door, one hand on the latch.
The sorting table is bare. Where the crate stood: a chalk mark, or a splintered, empty crate.

Not everyone stepped down with you, though you feel the missing at your shoulder.
Deliberate together, then cast your ballots. They are revealed all at once.

paragraphs: At Kingsgate two constables are waiting. Miss Vell holds out her burned hand for the cuffs, as if offering it to be read.
The constables listen, then shrug. Without proof she is free to go, hands in her pockets.
A warrant goes out by telegraph from Kingsgate. Somewhere beyond Harrow, a woman with a bandaged hand hears the wires sing.
Miss Vell tips her hat to you and is gone into the crowd. That winter the chronometer is patented, under her name.
“I built it. Every gear, every correction. He put his name on my work and meant to sell it tonight to pay his debts. I only wound his watch past the red mark. He did the rest himself.”
